name: US railroads, the first infrastructure bubble
trigger: Land grants and the telegraph making long distance freight and information cheap.
funding: Bonds, land grants, and speculative equity, with many lines oversubscribed before a single rail was laid.

phases.markers: Ports and canals at capacity, freight rates high, charters granted freely.
phases.outcome: Incumbent carriers and canal owners collect.

phases.markers: Mileage doubles, labor and iron shortages, bond issuance explodes, promoters paid in stock.
Parallel lines, rate wars, freight rates collapse, receiverships.
phases.outcome: Equity holders wiped out in successive panics.

phases.markers: A quarter of US rail mileage in receivership, consolidation into trunk systems.
Regulated rates, stable freight, consolidated trunk lines earn steady returns.

what_persisted: Freight demand and the physical network; the second owner of an asset bought at receiver prices.
what_died: The promotional equity and the first generation of parallel lines.

mapping_to_current.why: Capacity shortage, promotional capital, overbuild, consolidation is the same sequence.
Capex growth alone never identified the turning point, which is why phase markers are paired.

falsifier: Infrastructure cycles since then show no overbuild or shakeout phase.
source: US economic history literature on railroad panics and receiverships

name: Electrification and the utility holding company bubble
trigger: Cheap alternating current transmission made electricity a networked product.
funding: Holding company structures with layered debt, marketed to retail investors as a growth story.

phases.markers: City franchises scarce, electricity expensive, small isolated plants.
Generation and grid capex booms, holding companies acquire hundreds of utilities, pyramided leverage.
Capacity ahead of demand, rate competition, holding company leverage opaque.
Holding company collapse, defaults, Public Utility Holding Company Act breaking the pyramids.
Regulated rate base, stable allowed returns, utility becomes a bond-like asset.

what_persisted: The physical grid and the regulated compact.
what_died: Layered holding company leverage and the promotional marketing behind it.

mapping_to_current.why: Load growth to capex to rate base is the same regulated conversion that followed the bust.
Rate base economics are rate sensitive, which ties the analogue to our rates factor.

falsifier: The regulated compact fails to survive the current buildout where it held before.
source: utility holding company literature and the 1935 Act record

name: Merchant power and deregulation
trigger: Deregulation promised competitive generation markets and merchant plants earned development premiums.
funding: Project finance, high yield debt, and IPO windows for merchant developers.

phases.markers: California and other markets with reserve shortfalls, spark spreads wide.
Over 200GW announced, turbine slots scarce, developers IPO at premiums.
Reserve margins jump, spark spreads collapse, plants worth less than cost.
Calpine, Mirant, NRG and others restructure; assets sold at fractions of cost.
phases.outcome: Debt holders and buyers take assets.

phases.markers: Consolidated fleets with contracts, capacity markets formalised in ISOs.

what_persisted: Physical generation and the capacity market design that pays for standing still.
what_died: The merchant development premium and its high yield financing.

mapping_to_current.why: Turbine slot scarcity in the current cycle is the same marker as 1999-2002.
In the analogue, skilled construction labour priced up before the overbuild.

falsifier: Capacity markets and contracts fail to stabilise returns after the current overbuild.

name: The nuclear build and its cancellations
trigger: Utility demand growth forecasts and a technology seen as too cheap to meter.
funding: Regulated rate base and construction work in progress, with cost overruns eventually disallowed.

phases.markers: Demand growth strong, oil price risk, reactor orders surge.
phases.outcome: Vendors and utilities with early plants.

phases.markers: Order book peaks above 200 reactors, lead times stretch, cost estimates triple.
Demand growth halves after the oil shocks, plants arrive late and massively over budget.
phases.outcome: Utilities with construction work in progress carry the cost.

phases.markers: Cancellations of over 100 units, WPPSS default, prudence disallowances.
phases.outcome: Ratepayers and shareholders absorb the losses.

phases.markers: Completed plants run cheaply for decades, life extensions, uprates.
phases.outcome: Owners of completed plants earn durable margins.

what_persisted: Completed plants, and the lesson that late cost arrives after demand forecasts decay.
what_died: Construction work in progress and the demand forecasts underwriting it.

mapping_to_current.why: The current firm power contracts are the analogue's early phase, and the cancellation risk is phase 3.
Cost and schedule revisions are the analogue's central failure mode, which is exactly the object we measured.

falsifier: Modular construction and fixed price contracts remove the overrun mechanism.
source: US nuclear construction and cancellation record

name: The fiber and telecom bubble
trigger: The 1996 Telecom Act and the internet traffic forecasts of the late 1990s.
funding: High yield bonds, vendor financing from equipment makers, and equity at extraordinary multiples.

phases.markers: Long distance and internet capacity tight, incumbents profitable.
Long haul fiber mileage multiplied, equipment order books full, vendor financing hides demand quality.
Most installed fiber dark, bandwidth prices collapse over ninety percent, traffic forecasts missed by years.
Global Crossing, 360networks, WorldCom failures; equipment vendors restructure.
phases.outcome: Dark fiber bought at cents on the dollar.

phases.markers: Survivors and new entrants light the fiber for video and cloud traffic at low cost.
phases.outcome: Buyers of cheap assets earn the second wave.

what_persisted: The glass in the ground and the traffic that eventually used it.
what_died: The debt and the equipment vendor financing cycle.

mapping_to_current.why: Dark fiber is the analogue of dark interconnection capacity, bought cheap by the second wave.
Interconnect is that same physical layer in the current cycle.

falsifier: Current capacity additions are matched to demand with contracts that cannot reprice.
source: telecom bubble record and bandwidth price collapse data

name: Midstream MLPs and pipeline overbuild
trigger: Shale production growth needed gathering and takeaway capacity.
funding: MLP structures with distribution growth promises, funded by debt and equity issuance.

phases.markers: Takeaway constraints, basis differentials wide, gathering fees strong.
Capital spending multiples distributable cash flow, projects announced far ahead of volume.
Basin congestion reverses, fee compression, some pipelines underutilised at completion.
phases.outcome: Levered MLPs de-rate as distributions exceed cash flow.

phases.markers: Distribution cuts, consolidation into corporate structures, ESG-driven capital exit.
Consolidated midstream with buybacks and fee-based contracts, energy transition discount slowly lifts.
phases.outcome: Consolidators earn returns on cheap assets.

what_persisted: The pipes and the fee-based contracts on them.
what_died: The distribution growth promise and the leverage behind it.

mapping_to_current.why: The phase 4-5 value came from free cash flow discipline after growth died.
The shift to contracted, fee-like structures is the same second wave shape.

falsifier: Contracted take-or-pay structures prevent the overbuild repricing.
source: MLP era capital and distribution record

name: Cloud and colocation, the most recent analogue
trigger: Commodity server virtualization and the shift of enterprise IT to rented capacity.
funding: REIT conversions, venture capital for platforms, vendor financing from server makers.

phases.markers: Power-dense colocation scarce in primary markets, rents firm.
Hyperscaler self-build plus REIT acquisition, powered shell development booms.
Secondary market vacancies rise, rent concessions, wholesale leases at lower spreads.
Consolidation of small hosts, operator exits, asset sales.
Preleased hyperscale campuses, REIT structures with long contracts, dividends.

what_persisted: Land, power interconnections and the leasing contracts.

mapping_to_current.why: The current AI build is the same asset class entering its own phase 2.
Cooling density is the variable the cloud cycle largely did not have at scale, so the analogue is partial.

falsifier: Current build is fully preleased and self-funded, which would skip the speculative phase.
source: colocation REIT and cloud capex record

name: US LNG export buildout
trigger: Shale gas abundance and global demand for flexible molecules.
funding: 20 year take-or-pay contracts and project finance on contracted volumes.

phases.markers: Global LNG tight, Asian spot prices high, US projects queue for permits.
Train FIDs cluster, engineering and module yards saturated, long lead equipment booked.
phases.outcome: Engineers and early contract holders win.

phases.markers: Global liquefaction capacity grows faster than contracted demand, spot spreads compress.
phases.outcome: Contracted sellers protected, merchant volumes exposed.

phases.markers: Cancellations of speculative trains, consolidation of developers.
Fully contracted trains with stable tolling revenue.

what_persisted: The contracted tolling model that survived the price cycle.

mapping_to_current.why: Take-or-pay contracts are the analogue of firm power PPAs for data centers.
Engineer and module capacity were the binding constraint in phase 2.

falsifier: Contracted volumes cover all new capacity so no merchant exposure remains.

name: Offshore wind and the cable bottleneck
trigger: Decarbonisation targets and maturing fixed bottom technology.
funding: Contract for difference auctions, utility balance sheets, and supply chain credit.

phases.markers: Subsidy support strong, few capable installers, costs falling.
Cable and vessel capacity sells out years ahead, turbine prices firm, auction prices hit zero subsidy.
Cost inflation and financing rates break project economics, developers cancel contracted projects and write penalties.
Auction cancellations, supply chain losses, turbine maker writedowns.
phases.outcome: Owners of scarce inputs keep pricing power.

phases.markers: Indexed contracts pass cost through, consolidated supply chain.

what_persisted: The cable, vessel and port capacity, which re-priced upward through the bust.
what_died: Fixed price contracts written before cost inflation.

mapping_to_current.why: Cable ships and cables are the current cycle's analogue of scarce installation capacity.
Converter and valve capacity repeat the same bottlenecks.

falsifier: Supply chain capacity expands ahead of project awards so no bottleneck pricing appears.
source: offshore wind auction and supply chain record
